newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bread shortage adds to Bulgaria's economic woes.
newsitem.headline: Bread shortage adds to Bulgaria's economic woes.

text.p: Bread shortages added to Bulgaria's woes on Thursday as long queues formed outside bakeries from early morning and officials called for state wartime reserves to be urgently unblocked.
By noon, shelves were empty in most bakeries in the capital Sofia or were selling only biscuits and rolls.
"People were queuing from early in the morning and some were buying 10 loaves to keep in their refrigerators," said Gergana Ivanova, saleswoman in a private bakery.
The mill in Sofia stopped work last week and is using up its stocks of flour.

"We will not be able to secure the flour needed for bread unless the government urgently unblocks some 15,000 tonnes of wheat from the state wartime reserves," the mill's executive director Emil Zhivkov told a news conference.
Earlier this week officials said Bulgaria's bread wheat supplies would end in the next 15 to 20 days and the state reserve currently held only 30 percent of its usual supplies.
The caretaker government, which took office last week, has set up a special Grain Crisis Solution Council led by interim Prime Minister Stefan Sofianski.
After a cabinet session on Thursday, Sofianski confirmed that Bulgaria would use part of its wheat reserves and said it needed 450,000 tonnes of wheat to fill the gap until the new crop.
"We will ensure supplies probably through a scheme for importing wheat now against futures contracts to export the same quantity of wheat from the new crop," he added.
"We will try to lower the price which is $170-180 per tonne," said Sofianski.
Bread, a staple food of Bulgarians, is subsidised by the government.
Bulgaria is battling an acute grain shortage after uncontrolled exports two years ago depleted supplies. A poor harvest last year was attributed to bad weather and a lack of funds for fertilisers.

The crisis-ridded Balkan country also hopes to win funding from the European Union and other international lenders and governments and to receive some wheat as humanitarian aid, government officials said.
